title: When Does Refinancing Actually Make Sense?
description: Refinancing can lower your payment, shorten your loan, or remove mortgage insurance, but it isn't free. How to find your break-even point and decide.
image_alt: A white house surrounded by tall maple trees

faq.q: How do I calculate my refinance break-even point?
faq.a: Divide your total refinance costs by your monthly savings. The result is roughly how many months it takes to recover the cost.

faq.q: Is there a rule of thumb for how much rates need to drop?
faq.a: Rules of thumb are a starting point at best. Your loan balance, closing costs, and how long you'll keep the loan matter more than any single rate difference.

faq.q: Can I refinance to remove FHA mortgage insurance?
faq.a: Yes. Many homeowners refinance from FHA to a conventional loan once they have enough equity, which can eliminate FHA mortgage insurance.

body_html:
"Should I refinance?" is a question I answer almost every week, and the honest answer is always: it depends on your goal and your timeline. A refinance replaces your existing mortgage with a new one. That costs money up front, so it only makes sense when the benefits outweigh the costs within a timeframe that fits your plans.

Start with the goal

People refinance for different reasons, and each one has its own math:

  • Lower the monthly payment through a better rate or a different loan structure
  • Shorten the loan to pay it off sooner and reduce total interest
  • Remove mortgage insurance, often by moving from FHA to conventional
  • Switch from adjustable to fixed for payment stability
  • Access equity through a cash-out refinance
  • Remove a borrower after a divorce or change in ownership

The break-even calculation

For payment-focused refinances, the break-even point is the key number. Take your total refinance costs and divide by your monthly savings. The result is roughly how many months it takes to recover what you spent.

If you expect to keep the home and the loan well beyond that point, the refinance likely pays off. If you might sell or refinance again before then, it may not.

The right question isn't "Did rates drop?" It's "Will I keep this loan long enough to come out ahead?"

Costs people forget

CostWhy it matters
Lender and third-party feesAppraisal, title, escrow, and recording costs add up
PointsPaying points lowers the rate but lengthens the break-even
Prepaids and escrowYour new escrow account is funded, though your old one is refunded later
Restarting the clockA new full-length loan can mean more total interest even with a lower rate

That last point is the subtle one. If you're several years into your current mortgage, refinancing into a brand-new long-term loan resets the payoff date. Sometimes a shorter term, or making extra principal payments on the new loan, keeps you on track.

Refinancing to remove mortgage insurance

This is one of the most common wins I see. If your home has appreciated and you're on an FHA loan, a conventional refinance with enough equity can eliminate mortgage insurance entirely. If you're on a conventional loan with PMI, you may be able to request cancellation without refinancing at all. I explain the difference in this guide to PMI and MIP.

When to wait

  • You're planning to sell in the near future
  • Your credit took a recent hit that will recover in a few months
  • The savings are small relative to the costs
  • Your current loan has terms that would be hard to replace

A simple illustration

Here's a hypothetical example with round numbers, not a quote. Say a refinance costs $6,000 in total and lowers your monthly payment by $250. Divide $6,000 by $250 and the break-even point is 24 months. If you expect to keep the loan for five or more years, the refinance likely makes sense. If you're planning to sell in 18 months, it probably doesn't.

Now say the same refinance only saves $75 a month. The break-even stretches to 80 months, nearly seven years. That's a much harder case to make unless you're confident you'll stay put.

No-cost refinances

Some refinances are structured with lender credits that cover most or all closing costs in exchange for a slightly higher rate. These can make sense when the rate improvement is meaningful and you value flexibility. Your break-even is near zero, so you aren't locked into staying a long time to come out ahead. Ask your loan officer to price both a traditional and a no-cost option so you can compare.

The takeaway

A good refinance has a clear goal and a break-even point you'll comfortably pass. Get a Loan Estimate, compare it to your current loan line by line, and think honestly about how long you'll stay. If you're considering using equity at the same time, compare a cash-out refinance with a HELOC before deciding.
